questions.prompt: You run a container, write /tmp/result.txt inside it, then run docker rm on the container. What happens to the file?
options: It is lost, because it was in the container's writable layer
It is copied to the host automatically when the container is removed
It is kept if the container was stopped first, since stopping saves its files
It is kept in the image, which stores every file written by the container
questions.explanation: The writable layer is discarded when the container is removed.

questions.prompt: A named volume is mounted at /results. Where must the program write results so they survive replacing the container?
options: Under /app if the image contains it
questions.explanation: Only paths covered by a mount persist; everything else goes to the writable layer.

questions.prompt: Which statement about an image and a container is correct?
options: A container is a template for images; each image is created by running a container
An image is a read-only template; a container is an instance with a writable layer
Images and containers are the same thing, only named differently in the tools
An image is a running process that holds a writable layer of its own
questions.explanation: Containers are created from images and add a writable layer and a running process.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile has 6 instructions. Editing one source file changes the 5th instruction (COPY . .). How many layers/instructions are taken from the cache? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: Instructions 1-4 are unchanged and cached; the 5th and everything after are rebuilt.

questions.prompt: Why copy requirements.lock and run pip install before copying the rest of the code?
options: It makes the final image smaller by definition, since fewer layers are stored
Docker requires lock files to be copied first, or the build fails
Pip can only run before any code has been copied into the image
Code changes then do not invalidate the cached dependency layer
questions.explanation: The first changed instruction invalidates all later ones; dependencies change rarely, code often.

questions.prompt: Three images share a 120 MB base layer. Each adds its own 30 MB layer. How many MB of storage do the three images need in total? (integer, tolerance 0.5)
questions.explanation: Shared layers are stored once: 120 + 3×30 = 210 MB.

questions.prompt: You must show a reviewer which files of your experiment survive when the container is replaced with a new version of the image. Describe the experiment, the commands, and what you will observe.
rubric: Writes one file into a mounted volume and one into the container filesystem (e.g. /tmp), then docker rm.
Starts a new container with the same volume and lists both paths; also uses docker diff/ls to observe.
Observes only the volume file survives; read-only mounts reject writes; records the image digest and notes that the kernel/driver is not packaged.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
